eligibility_reason: The Operator maps incoming document observations to intermediate semantic structures and the Reconciler writes these into a persistent workspace that enforces temporal, spatial, and logical coherence as new input arrives (p. 1, Introduction: 'Our framework comprises an Operator ... and a Reconciler, which integrates these into a persistent workspace'; p. 2 gives a worked example of the resulting memory trace). That workspace is later read back at query time: an NER pass on the query is matched to entity-specific summaries held in the workspace, which are then re-ranked and passed to an answering LLM (Fig. 11, p. 20) — a run-time write followed by later retrieval that conditions the system's subsequent output, satisfying I1. This is exactly the run-time-write-added-to-a-RAG-pipeline case the guide instructs to include rather than treat as fixed-corpus retrieval (E3): the workspace content is generated by the Operator/Reconciler, not a static pre-built index. I2/I3/I4 hold: 2025 record (arXiv header p. 1), English throughout, text provided.

facets.justification: The given pages describe the workspace's contents (entity/role/spatiotemporal frames, p. 1-2) and its retrieval mechanics (NER + string match to 'GSW instances', then embedding re-rank, Fig. 11 p. 20), but not its underlying storage implementation. Section 2, where the Operator/Reconciler architecture and the workspace's data structure would be specified, was not among the extracted pages (only pages 1, 2, 20, 21, 23, 26, 27, 28 of 28 were given), so I cannot decide between vector_store, graph_store, or another structured form without guessing.

The worked example on p. 2 shows the Operator/Reconciler condensing a document passage into a compact structured entity record ('Carter Stewart; Role: a researcher and presenter; Location: Bethpage Black Course; Date: March 23, 2024, Did What?: Presented his research findings...'), and the QA trace on p. 20 shows the store literally holding per-chapter 'Summary:' entries for each entity that are retrieved and re-ranked. The stored units are condensed representations of the source narrative, not synthesized content absent from any single source passage.

Figure 11 (p. 20) states the pipeline explicitly: entities extracted by NER are matched to relevant GSW instances 'via string matching' (a structured lookup), the retrieved entity summaries are then 're-ranked based on their semantic similarity to the input query — a score calculated using cosine similarity between their embeddings and the query's embedding.' This is a declared two-stage combination (structured match, then similarity re-rank), matching the guide's requirement of a stated fusion/re-ranking rule for hybrid.

The paper's own evaluation is entirely benchmark-based: EpBench-200 and EpBench-2000 with bootstrap-resampled error bars against RAG baselines (Table 12, p. 23), plus an ablation on a short-book variant and an Operator-vs-semantic-parsing-baseline human preference study (Tables 10, 15, p. 21 and p. 27). No deployed system, real users, or fielded use is reported anywhere in the given pages, so this is validation, not evaluation.

Table 12 (p. 23) reports precision/recall/F1 for GSW against four baselines (Embedding RAG, GraphRAG, HippoRAG2, LightRAG) across EpBench-2000 cue-complexity buckets, and p. 21 describes the EpBench-200/2000 main evaluation protocol with bootstrap resampling over 1,000 iterations — a fixed task suite with reported scores across systems.

The paper repeatedly names its contribution an architecture, not merely a technique: 'we propose the Generative Semantic Workspace (GSW), a neuro-inspired generative memory framework' (p. 1 abstract), and Section 2 is titled 'The Generative Semantic Workspace (GSW) Framework' (p. 2), describing the two-component Operator/Reconciler organisation the rest of the paper argues for.
